name: Ndonde Hamba
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: First, it was shown that the final syllable of every word is extraprosodic, and with the exception of a single tense, rules never assign tone to, or even see, the final syllable at the word-level. Stress and noncontrastive (but linguistically significant) vowel length are automatically assigned to the penultimate syllable of all words. The following rule assigns a second mora to stressed syllables. (1) Stress Lengthening ... Only the stress of the last word in an utterance is phonetically realized in connected speech, so we assume that medial stresses are either severely reduced or eliminated altogether.
new_statements.citation: Odden, David. 1990. Tone in the Makonde dialects: Chimahuta. Studies in African Linguistics 21(2): 149-188.
new_statements.locator: sec.1 Introduction, pp.149-150 (rule (1) Stress Lengthening); also fn.8 p.176
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (40 pp., text; SAL 21(2), open access at journals.flvc.org). The quoted passage is on pp.149-150 exactly as given ('First, it was shown that the final syllable of every word is extraprosodic.. Stress and noncontrastive (but linguistically significant) vowel length are automatically assigned to the penultimate syllable of all words. The following rule assigns a second mora to stressed syllables. (1) Stress Lengthening [diagram] Only the stress of the last word in an utterance is phonetically realized in connected speech, so we assume that medial stresses are either severely reduced or eliminated altogether.'); the '..' only skips the autosegmental diagram of rule (1). Footnote…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word is stressed on its penultimate syllable (the final syllable is extraprosodic); the stressed penult is lengthened to two moras, there being no lexical length contrast. In connected speech only the last word of the utterance shows the stress/lengthening phonetically; medial stresses are reduced or lost.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement (one tense lets tone rules see the final syllable, but stress stays penultimate). Tone (fall vs level vs rise on the long penult) is assigned by tense-dependent rules and is independent of stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Odden assigns stress to every word but says it is phonetically realized only on the utterance-final word (fn.8 p.176: phrase-medial stress and length exist 'at a more abstract level' and are 'eliminated' later). Kraal 2005 (p.32, sec.3.5.1) and Leach 2010 describe the same surface fact for Makonde generally as PenUltimate Lengthening of the phonological-phrase-final word, 'not a stress-induced rule'; citation forms count as phrase-final and always show the long penult (Kraal's Chindonde forms kuulya 'to eat', mavaala 'shoulders', p.74). The catalog's mako1251 entry codes this as phrasal penult; the same choice would apply here.
new_statements.identity_note: ndon1252 'Ndonde Hamba' [njd] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid: Glottolog rules it 'a dialect of the language in the Makonde [kde] entry' (mako1251), citing Kraal 2005 and Crosse-Upcott 1956. The quoted stress statement is Odden 1990b on the 'Chimahuta' dialect of Tanzanian Makonde, which Kraal 2005:3 (and Leach 2010 sec.1.3.2 after him) identifies with the Chindonde (= Ndonde, Guthrie P.24) dialect of the south-western Makonde plateau (Kraal's Chindonde informant: Newala District). Caveat: the community Ethnologue names 'Ndonde Hamba' (Lindi Region, coordinates in SW Nachingwea District) matches Crosse-Upcott's 'neo-Hamba.. Ndonde speakers' of Kilimarondo, whom he classes as a KiNgindo-speaking (P.14, ngin1244) outlier, and Kraal himself says the Ndonde near Liwale/coast speak Ngindo, not Makonde; Gromova & Urb (2015-2020), the only modern fieldworkers on the Nachingwea Ndonde (c.2,500 speakers), treat it as a separate, Makonde-like P.24 language and publish no phonology. So the statement is first-hand for Chindonde/Chimahuta Makonde; its applicability to the Nachingwea 'Ndonde Hamba' community rests on Glottolog's equation. mako1251 is already in the catalog (Manus 2010, phrasal penult); this entry would be a dialect-level duplicate of that languoid.

sources.note: pp.149-150: stress and non-contrastive vowel length are automatically assigned to the penultimate syllable of all words (final syllable extraprosodic; Stress Lengthening adds a mora); only the stress of the last word in an utterance is phonetically realized, medial stresses reduced or eliminated. Fn.8 p.176: phrase-medial words get stress/length abstractly, realized only utterance-finally.

sources.citation: Leach, Michael Benjamin. 2010. Things Hold Together: Foundations for a systemic treatment of verbal and nominal tone in Plateau Shimakonde. LOT 260. Utrecht: LOT.
sources.note: sec.1.3.2: 'Kraal identifies Ndonde as an alternative name for the Chimahuta dialect (referred to by Nurse 1979 and Odden 1990a/b)'; fn.2 relation of Chimahuta/Chindonde (TZ) to Shindoonde (MZ) needs research. Stress statement (p.330, penult length marks p-phrase boundary) is for Plateau Shimakonde, not Ndonde.

sources.citation: Kraal, Pieter J. 2005. A Grammar of Makonde (Chinnima, Tanzania). PhD dissertation, Leiden University. Chapter 1, Introduction (pp.1-15). hdl.handle.net/1887/4271.
sources.note: Identity only: pp.2-3 'Ndonde (P.24) does not exist as a separate language.. it is the name of one of the dialects of the Makonde of Tanzania [Chindonde]'; 'We differ from Nurse and Odden in that they applied the name Chimahuta to what we call Chindonde'; Ndonde near Liwale and on the coast are Ngindo-speaking, not Makonde. Chindonde informant from Newala District.

sources.citation: Odden, David. 1990. Tone in the Makonde dialects: Chimaraba. Studies in African Linguistics 21(1): 61-105.
sources.note: p.62 reports Nurse 1979: 'in Makonde, nouns have penultimate stress, and verbs have stress whose position varies according to verb tense'; lists five dialects incl. Chimahuta; pp.63-64 penult stress + Stress Lengthening for Chimaraba (not the Ndonde dialect).
